q: Pale rosado drawn from black and white grapes picked and fermented together made one Castilian denomination's name long before its reds did. Which one?
exp: The old field blend was co-fermented rather than blended afterwards, which gives a paler and more savoury wine than a modern rosado bled off a red vat. Cigales sits between Ribera del Duero and Toro on the Pisuerga, and its reds have only lately caught up with the pink wine that carried the name for centuries.

q: Putting Verdejo on a Rueda label commits a bodega to more of the grape than the denomination name alone does. Give the minimum a varietal label demands.
accept: at least eighty five percent verdejo
a minimum of eighty five percent verdejo
a minimum of eighty five percent
exp: Plain Rueda needs half the blend to be Verdejo and the rest may be Viura or another permitted white; naming the grape lifts the floor. The same figure governs a Rueda labelled Sauvignon, so the two claims on a shelf are stronger than they look and the unnamed bottle is the one to ask about.

q: White vines are scattered through the oldest Ribera del Duero plantings, and the denomination now authorises a white wine from the local one. Name that variety.
exp: It was interplanted among the black vines for centuries and a little of it still finds its way into the reds, softening them without lifting the colour. Albillo Real, grown around Madrid, is a different variety altogether despite the shared first name, and the confusion is exactly why the rulebook spells out which Albillo it means.

q: Downstream of Toro the Duero cuts a granite gorge along the Portuguese border, and the denomination there is built on Juan Garcia. Name it.
exp: The gorge shelters terraces that would be unworkable anywhere colder, and Juan Garcia gives a pale, high-toned red closer to a Galician wine than to anything in Castile. Port country begins a short way downstream, where the same gorge carries on into Portugal, so the hard rock and the vertiginous terracing are of a piece with what follows.

q: A downy-leaved mutation of Garnacha holds its acidity better in heat, and the Catalan rulebooks list it separately from its parent. What is it called?
exp: The underside of the leaf is felted with fine hairs, which is where the name comes from, and growers keep it on the hottest and stoniest parcels because it ripens more slowly than ordinary Garnacha. It is permitted across the Catalan denominations and is a fair share of the old-vine plantings a buyer is actually paying for when a label says Garnacha.

q: In Alella, north of Barcelona, the local white goes by Pansa Blanca. Which widely planted Catalan variety is that?
accept: xarel lo also called pansa blanca
exp: One vine, two names, and the Alella version is the older of them. Xarel-lo is the most oxidation-resistant of the traditional Catalan whites, which is why it carries the body in a sparkling blend and why it is the one of them most often bottled on its own as a still wine. Watch the pink-skinned Xarel-lo Vermell, a separate variety that Alella calls Pansa Rosada, because the two Pansas are as easy to confuse as the two names of this one.

q: Growers took Bierzo's red for a relative of Cabernet Franc until DNA profiling settled the question. What did the profiling show?
opts: It is a colour mutation of Godello, the white grown on the same slopes
It is the same variety as Portugal's Jaen
It is identical to Galicia's Brancellao under a Leonese name
It is a natural crossing of Tempranillo and Garnacha from the Middle Ages
exp: The Cabernet Franc idea came from the perfume, all violet and graphite, rather than from anything in the vine, and it was repeated in print for decades. Jaen is grown in the Dao, across the mountains from Bierzo, and the match tells you the variety crossed the border long before anyone was recording what they planted.

q: East on the Leon plateau a thick-skinned black grape gives deeply coloured rosados, made by dropping whole bunches into the fermenting must. Name the variety.
exp: The technique is called madreo, and the added bunches restart the ferment and raise a light prickle that the wine keeps into the bottle. The variety takes its name from its dark, pointed berries, its bunches are unusually compact, and it is grown seriously almost nowhere outside the province. A white mutation of it exists and is a different grape, so the rulebooks name the black one in full.

q: One Galician denomination lies inland against the Portuguese border in a sheltered valley, and it is the warmest and driest of the five. Which?
exp: The valley of the Tamega sits in a rain shadow, so Monterrei ripens Godello and Treixadura with far less anxiety about rot than the coast has. It is the least exported of the five and the one a Galician list is least likely to carry, which is exactly why it is worth asking about.

q: Facing Portugal across the mouth of the Mino, one Rias Baixas subzone traditionally blends Loureira into its Albarino. Name the subzone.
exp: The blend gives a more floral and slightly softer wine than the pure Albarino of the northern subzones, and the terraces there run down to the river rather than to the open Atlantic. Condado do Tea, further upstream, is the warmest of the subzones and Val do Salnes on the coast is the coolest, so the appellation spans a real climatic range for so small a place.

q: Inland along the Avia and the Mino, the Ribeiro leans on a later-ripening native that gives more flesh and less bite than Albarino. Name it.
exp: It buds and ripens late, needs a warmer inland site than the coast can offer, and gives a broader wine usually blended with Godello, Loureira or Torrontes. In northern Portugal the same vine is Trajadura and goes into Vinho Verde for exactly the same reason: weight.

q: Printing Albarino on the front of a Rias Baixas bottle triggers a stricter rule than leaving it off. How much of the grape must the wine then hold?
accept: it must be one hundred percent albarino
exp: Nothing else may be in the blend, which is a stricter varietal rule than most of Europe uses and is why the name on the front is worth reading. A Rias Baixas without the grape name may perfectly well be a blend with Loureira, Caino Blanco or Treixadura, and in the southern subzones it usually is.

q: A butt fortified past a certain strength loses its veil of flor for good and turns oxidative. Roughly where does that line fall?
opts: Around 12 percent, which is the strength of the unfortified base wine
exp: The yeast that forms the veil stops working somewhere close to fifteen and a half, so a cellar master fortifies to just under that line to keep a wine biological and to just over it to kill the flor deliberately. That single decision, taken on a young wine, is what separates the whole Fino family from the whole Oloroso family.

q: Wine drawn off the solera row is topped back up from the criadera above it, in an operation the bodegas name after dew. Give that term.
exp: The word is literal: the younger wine is introduced gently, down the wall of the butt or through a tube, so the veil floating on the surface is not torn. Tearing it would let oxygen at the wine underneath, which is the one thing a biological cellar exists to prevent, and it is why the refill is a slow job rather than a pour.

q: A cellar hand lifts a sample from beneath the veil without tearing it, using a narrow cup on a long whippy handle. Name the tool.
exp: The Jerez form is a silver cup on a whalebone or cane rod, long enough to reach the bottom of a butt through the bunghole; Sanlucar uses a lighter one cut from a single piece of cane. The person wielding it is the venenciador, and pours from arm's height into a glass held at the waist, which aerates the wine and is a good deal harder than it looks.

q: One outstanding harvest is set aside and aged in its own casks, never refreshed from a younger scale. What is a Sherry made that way called?
exp: It carries a year on the label, which almost nothing else in Jerez does, because a solera has no vintage to declare. The wines were traditionally kept in the coolest corner of the bodega and drawn on to correct a solera in a difficult year, so bottling one at all is a modern decision rather than an old tradition.
